messages.author: 3cfd637695216907
messages.subject: large arrays of transformed parameters
parts:
Hi all - 

Newbie to both Stan and BUGS (it's been pretty fun so far). I'm exploring conversion of an existing BUGS model to Stan. (More precisely, I'm using rjags and RStan.) One section in the BUGS code models input data r as a normal variable parameterized in terms of a design matrix and some unobserved parameters a (scalar) and b (vector), as follows: 


# BUGS

for (i in 1:n) {
    r[i] ~ dnorm(r.hat[i], tau)
    r.hat[i] <- a + b %*% model.matrix[i,]
}

a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
for (i in 1:length(model.matrix[1,])) {
    b[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
}
tau <- pow(sigma, -2)
sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)


I translated into Stan as follows: 

// Stan

data {
    int n;
    int n_factors;
    real r[n];
}
parameters {
    real a;
    real b[n_factors];
}
transformed parameters {
    real r_hat[n];
    for (i in 1:n) {
        r_hat[i] <- a;
        for (j in 1:n_factors)
            r_hat[i] <- r_hat[i] + b[j] * model_matrix[i,j];
    }
}
model {
    a ~ normal(0, 100);
    b ~ normal(0, 1);
    r ~ normal(r_hat, sigma);
    sigma ~ uniform(0, 100);
}


So I ended up with a (transformed) parameter r_hat for every observation, and n was about 14000 in my case. This appeared to slow things down considerably; it ran much more quickly when I stored only unique model_matrix rows (a drastically smaller number) and had only one r_hat per unique row, and then recreated a longer vector to pass to r in the model blok. 

Is this something specific to watch out for when coding a model in Stan vs. BUGS coding - large arrays in the parameters or transformed parameters blocks slow things down a lot? If so, why does this appear, at least on first glance, to be not as big of a deal with BUGS? 

thanks
Andy

On Thursday, June 27, 2013 6:06:07 PM UTC-4, Andrew Lim wrote:
I translated into Stan as follows: 

// Stan

data {
    int n;
    int n_factors;
    real r[n];
}
parameters {
    real a;
    real b[n_factors];
}
transformed parameters {
    real r_hat[n];
    for (i in 1:n) {
        r_hat[i] <- a;
        for (j in 1:n_factors)
            r_hat[i] <- r_hat[i] + b[j] * model_matrix[i,j];
    }
}
model {
    a ~ normal(0, 100);
    b ~ normal(0, 1);
    r ~ normal(r_hat, sigma);
    sigma ~ uniform(0, 100);
}


So I ended up with a (transformed) parameter r_hat for every observation, and n was about 14000 in my case. This appeared to slow things down considerably; it ran much more quickly when I stored only unique model_matrix rows (a drastically smaller number) and had only one r_hat per unique row, and then recreated a longer vector to pass to r in the model blok.

Your post left out the declaration of model_matrix (and sigma), but it think you can just do

r ~ normal(a + model_matrix * b, sigma);

Is this something specific to watch out for when coding a model in Stan vs. BUGS coding - large arrays in the parameters or transformed parameters blocks slow things down a lot? If so, why does this appear, at least on first glance, to be not as big of a deal with BUGS?

Certainly large arrays in the parameters block would tend to be slow because then you have a lot of parameters that Stan needs to track the gradient of. A large array in transformed parameters or locally in the model block usually isn't a major time suck compared to the auto-differentiation. However, if you do it in transformed parameters, then it has to write a lot of columns in the csv file. In most cases, the linear predictor isn't interesting enough to store and if it were needed, then it could easily be reconstructed in R afterward.

You do want to utilize matrix algebra whenever possible because those operations tend to be those where someone (usually Marcus) has done some performance optimizations. But that holds no matter what block you do it in.
 
Ben

On 6/27/13 6:44 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, June 27, 2013 6:06:07 PM UTC-4, Andrew Lim wrote:

> Certainly large arrays in the parameters block would tend to be slow because then you have a lot of parameters that Stan
> needs to track the gradient of. A large array in transformed parameters or locally in the model block usually isn't a
> major time suck compared to the auto-differentiation.

Right. But the transformed parameters do add auto-diff variables
to the stack (and hence cause constructors to be called and a virtual
function to be called during autodiff). But in this case, these would
have to be calculated anyway for the linear predictors.

> However, if you do it in transformed parameters, then it has to
> write a lot of columns in the csv file. In most cases, the linear predictor isn't interesting enough to store and if it
> were needed, then it could easily be reconstructed in R afterward.
>
> You do want to utilize matrix algebra whenever possible because those operations tend to be those where someone (usually
> Marcus) has done some performance optimizations. But that holds no matter what block you do it in.

It's mainly an issue for auto-diff variables (parameters, transformed
parameters, or local variables in transformed parameters or model).

- Bob
